introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Food and Nutrition 2 (0540), ORDINARY LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ANY FOUR QUESTIONS.

You are reminded of the necessity of good English and orderly presentation of work. Tabulate wherever possible and use diagrams where appropriate.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde imprime « ANSWER ANY FOUR QUESTIONS » (4 sur 6 questions imprimées), sans section et sans mention « only the first four will be marked ». `groupes` = ["PAPER 2"] et `regles_choix` = parmi 4 sur 6, identiques dans les 6 fichiers.

Sujet scanné de 3 pages (page de garde, questions 1 à 4, questions 5 et 6), lu en image ; aucun schéma ni figure imprimé, donc `figures` vide dans tous les fichiers. Filigranes (gcerevision.com, Kawlo) ignorés. L'en-tête imprimé « Food And Nutrition 2 » est recopié en « Food and Nutrition 2 » dans l'introduction.

Points : chaque question imprime « Total = (25 marks) » ; les points imprimés des sous-questions totalisent bien 25 pour chacune des 6 questions (aucun écart). Pour 2(a), 5(a) et 6(b), `points` de la sous-question est la somme des parties (i) et (ii) imprimées (2+5, 2+5, 3+5).

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au nombre exact d'éléments demandés. D'autres réponses sont valables pour les questions de liste ; le barème d'un point par élément est une hypothèse (le sujet ne le détaille pas). Aucune teneur nutritive chiffrée n'est avancée, sauf l'énergie d'un gramme de lipide (environ 37 kJ, valeur du programme).

Question 1(e) « mechanical raising agents » : le programme n'en nomme usuellement que deux (l'air et la vapeur), le sujet en demande quatre. Le corrigé donne quatre procédés mécaniques distincts (air par tamisage, par crémage, par fouettage, et vapeur) ; d'autres manuels répondent autrement (battage, pliage, laminage). À relire par un enseignant de Food and Nutrition.

Faits de cours à relire par un enseignant : les objectifs alimentaires de 5(b) (le sujet n'en impose aucun), les causes de faible production de 5(c) et les points de 6(d) sont des listes de manuel ; plusieurs autres réponses seraient acceptées.

Fautes d'impression du sujet recopiées telles quelles : « five (5) importance » au singulier (1d, 2a ii, 2d, 4d), « (5marks) », « (8marks) », « Recall three (3) advantages », « Pick out three (3) advantages ... of microwave cooking » sans point final, « Outline three (3) advantages and two (2) disadvantages of boiling » sans point final, « Define invitation ».

questions.enonce_markdown:
State five (5) factors that affect the availability of Vitamin C in food.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is easily lost from food. Five factors that affect how much of it is still available when the food is eaten (1 mark each):

1. **Heat (cooking).** Vitamin C is destroyed by heat, so long or strong cooking leaves little of it in the food.
2. **Solubility in water.** Vitamin C dissolves in water, so it is lost into the cooking water or washing water when vegetables are boiled, soaked or washed after cutting.
3. **Exposure to air (oxidation).** Oxygen in the air destroys vitamin C, so it is lost when vegetables and fruits are cut up, grated or mashed and left standing before they are cooked or eaten.
4. **Storage and freshness.** The longer fruits and vegetables are stored (or the longer cooked food is kept hot), the more vitamin C is lost; fresh food contains more than stale or wilted food.
5. **Alkaline conditions.** Adding bicarbonate of soda (an alkali) to green vegetables destroys vitamin C.

(Other correct points: preparing food a long time before cooking, peeling too thickly, drying or canning, and exposure to light or to copper and iron utensils.)
themes: vitamins and mineral salts in food

questions.enonce_markdown:
Describe five (5) strategies that can help an individual to lose weight.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A person puts on weight when the energy eaten is greater than the energy used by the body. Weight is lost when the energy eaten is **less** than the energy used. Five strategies (1 mark each):

1. **Eat smaller portions and avoid over-eating.** Reducing the quantity of food eaten lowers the energy taken in, and eating slowly helps the person to feel full sooner.
2. **Cut down on fatty and sugary foods.** Fried foods, pastries, sweets and sugary drinks are rich in energy; they are replaced by foods that give less energy for the same quantity.
3. **Eat more fruits, vegetables and fibre-rich foods.** Fruits, vegetables, whole cereals and beans fill the stomach and give little energy, so the person is satisfied without taking in too much energy.
4. **Take regular exercise.** Walking, running, sports or active work use up energy and make the body burn its stored fat.
5. **Choose low-fat methods of cooking and eat regular meals.** Boiling, steaming and grilling are used instead of deep frying, and meals are not skipped (skipping meals leads to snacking and over-eating later). Drinking water instead of sugary drinks also helps.

(Other correct points: keeping a food diary, setting a realistic target of slow weight loss, getting enough sleep, and seeing a doctor or dietitian for advice.)
themes: energy from food and body metabolism

questions.enonce_markdown:
List three positive and three negative effects of spices in the body.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Spices** are strong-flavoured parts of plants (seeds, bark, roots, buds) such as pepper, ginger, cloves and nutmeg, used in small quantities to flavour food.

| | Effects of spices in the body (1 mark each) |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | 1. They stimulate the appetite and the flow of saliva and digestive juices, so food is eaten with pleasure and digested more easily. |
| | 2. Some spices relieve digestive discomfort (ginger helps against nausea, some spices help against wind or flatulence). |
| | 3. Some have a soothing or antiseptic action (ginger and garlic are used against colds and sore throats). |
| **Negative** | 1. Too much hot spice irritates the lining of the mouth, stomach and intestine, and can cause heartburn or stomach pain, and can worsen ulcers. |
| | 2. In some people they cause allergic reactions (rash, swelling, sneezing). |
| | 3. Eaten in excess they cause diarrhoea, sweating and an uncomfortable burning feeling. |

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify five (5) importance of salad in a menu.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **salad** is a dish of raw (or cold cooked) vegetables and/or fruits, served with or without a dressing. Five reasons why it is important in a menu (1 mark each):

1. **It supplies vitamins and mineral salts**, especially vitamin C, which is not destroyed because the vegetables are eaten raw.
2. **It provides fibre (roughage)** which prevents constipation and helps digestion.
3. **It adds colour, variety and an attractive appearance** to the meal, which makes it more appetising.
4. **It adds contrast of texture and flavour** (crisp, fresh and juicy) to soft or rich main dishes.
5. **It is light and low in energy**, so it is useful in the diet of people who want to control their weight; it is also quick to prepare because no cooking is needed.

(Other correct points: it can be served as a starter, a side dish or a main course, and it can use left-over foods.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
List four (4) mechanical raising agents.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **raising agent** makes a cake or pastry rise by putting a gas into the mixture. **Mechanical** raising agents do not need a chemical or yeast: **air** and **steam** are used, and air is put into the mixture by physical action. Four mechanical raising agents/methods (1 mark each):

1. **Air by sieving** - sieving the flour (and raising agent) lets air into the dry ingredients.
2. **Air by creaming** - beating fat and sugar together traps air in the mixture (as in a Victoria sandwich cake).
3. **Air by whisking** - whisking eggs (or eggs and sugar) traps a large quantity of air in the foam (as in a sponge).
4. **Steam** - when a mixture with a lot of liquid (choux pastry, batter, puff pastry) is baked in a hot oven, the water turns to steam, which expands and makes the mixture rise.

(Other ways of putting air in: folding, rolling and rubbing in the fat. The main mechanical raising agents are air and steam.)
